newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova's new leader promises peace, prosperity.
newsitem.headline: Moldova's new leader promises peace, prosperity.

text.p: Moldovan parliament chairman Petru Lucinschi, winner of Sunday's presidential election run-off, said on Monday his four-year term would bring stability and prosperity to open up the former Soviet republic to the world.

"I will not be the president who divides people into good and bad, into democrats and communists, patriots and non-patriots," the 56-year-old former secretary of the Soviet Communist party Central Committee told reporters.

"Only political and social stability will allow us to speed up reforms...and raise living standards," he said at his first news conference as president-elect. He will take over from defeated President Mircea Snegur on January 15.

Lucinschi, who ran as an independent social democrat but was backed by a number of leftist parties including the communists, said he hoped a new coalition government could continue gradual market reforms.

Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, who was knocked out of the first round of voting on November 17, repeated on Monday that his government would resign after the election but asked ministers to work on until parliament accepted the resignation.
Sangheli has had the support of parliament but was bitterly opposed by Snegur.

"The new government will be formed on the basis of professionalism and honesty," said Lucinschi, adding he would form a cabinet of "national trust" that could include social democrats, liberals, communists and other parties.
He refused, however, to say whom he might nominate as prime minister or when he would form his government. Parliament must approve his new administration.

"We will continue integration in Europe, but will also strengthen traditional ties with our good neighbours -- Ukraine and Russia," said Lucinschi, a tall, bespectacled intellectual who presents himself a moderate.
Lucinschi, who is popular with Moldova's 35 percent minority of Russian-speakers, said he viewed relations with the majority's ethnic kin in Romania primarily as economic ones.

Snegur's moves towards "spiritual and cultural" integration with Bucharest alienated Moldova's mostly Slav 700,000-strong Dnestr region along the Ukrainian border, which broke away in 1990 fearing a possible merger with Romania.
Ties with Russia, on which Moldova heavily depends for supplies of most of its fuel and energy, may be a priority.
Lucinschi, who boasts of good contacts in the Kremlin, said: "I will use my ties in Moscow for the good of the country. Believe me, this is a very big advantage."

The president-elect said he would use these connections not just to allow energy-starved Moldova to survive the winter by buying yet more Russian fuel on credit, but also to resolve major political issues.

He wants to speed up the ratification by the Russian parliament of the 1990 basic treaty on relations between Moldova and Russia, as well as of a 1994 agreement on the pullout of Russia's 6,000-strong military forces from Dnestr.
"As for the Dnestr dispute, I hope to resolve it in line with the country's constitution and it will remain an inalienable part of Moldova," he said.
